---
title: "GC/MS deconvolution"
description: "Separate overlapping compounds into log-concave elution profiles and full mass spectra."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

`GCMSdeco()` takes a chromatogram from an ANDI-MS `.cdf` file to resolved
compound profiles, integrated areas and a NIST-compatible `.msp` spectral
library. Its `splogconNMF()` backend combines sparse selection with local
nonnegative factorization: narrow peaks and broad asymmetric peaks can each
be represented by a single log-concave profile. A smooth background is fitted
jointly, while every original mass channel is retained in the final spectra.

The [single and multichannel deconvolution tutorial](deconvolution.html)
introduces selection with a fixed peak shape. Here the peak shapes are refined
as part of the factorization, which is particularly useful for overloaded
or shark-fin-shaped peaks.

## Two experimental chromatograms

The package includes a cuticular-hydrocarbon window with six co-eluting
compounds (`GCMS_data1`, 119 scans × 671 mass channels) and a beer-headspace
window with a prominent broad acid peak (`GCMS_data2`, 1,764 scans × 518
mass channels). Their row names give retention times in minutes; column names
give nominal m/z. Both examples keep all mass channels.

```r
library(L0glm)
data(GCMS_data1)
data(GCMS_data2)

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "L0glm-GCMS")
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_GCMS_cdf(GCMS_data1, file.path(out, "GCMS_data1.cdf"))
write_GCMS_cdf(GCMS_data2, file.path(out, "GCMS_data2.cdf"))
```

`write_GCMS_cdf()` preserves the intensity matrix, including silent ions,
and writes scan times in seconds for ANDI-MS readers. The same `GCMSdeco()`
call then works with a matrix exported from R or a chromatogram exported by
instrument software:

```r
fit1 <- GCMSdeco(file.path(out, "GCMS_data1.cdf"),
  file.path(out, "GCMS_data1.msp"), nwindows = 1L, precluster = 16L,
  baseline_df = 1L,
  correlation = "none", ncores = 8L,
  psf_control = list(kernel_est = convkernel("gaussian", 65L,
    list(sigma = 8)), maxiter = 0L))

fit2 <- GCMSdeco(file.path(out, "GCMS_data2.cdf"),
  file.path(out, "GCMS_data2.msp"), nwindows = 1L, precluster = 32L,
  correlation = "none", ncores = 8L,
  psf_control = list(kernel_est = convkernel("gaussian", 65L,
    list(sigma = 6)), maxiter = 0L))

fit1$compounds
GIC(fit2)
coef(fit2, normalize = "l1")       # unit-area spectra in all 518 channels
```

These short windows use a supplied Gaussian PSF as the initial profile
dictionary. `maxiter=0L` keeps this PSF fixed; `splogconNMF()` then refines the
individual compound profiles. For a full chromatogram, the default
`nwindows=10L` with positive `maxiter` estimates a smoothly varying PSF.
An alkane standard can supply its initial calibration through
`alkanes_file="alkanes.cdf"`.
The hydrocarbon window uses a constant background; the longer beer window
uses the automatically chosen low-df cubic spline.

### Estimate the PSF automatically

`estimate_psf()` provides one interface for standard calibration and blind
sample estimation. Both bundled matrices include a full alkane TIC in
`attr(Y, "alkanes_TIC")`; its numeric names give retention times in minutes.
The estimator uses this calibration automatically, resamples to the sample
scan interval and refines the PSF on the sample:

```r
psf <- estimate_psf(GCMS_data2, nwindows = 3L)
X <- psf$X                         # sparse scan-by-scan PSF design
psf$width_scans

# A constant PSF, calibration alone, or blind fitting without a standard:
constant <- estimate_psf(GCMS_data2, nwindows = 1L)
standard <- estimate_psf(GCMS_data2, method = "standard", nwindows = 3L)
blind <- estimate_psf(GCMS_data2, standard = NULL, method = "blind",
  nwindows = 3L, precluster = 32L)
```

`precluster=FALSE` uses all ion channels, `1L` uses their total, and `32L`
uses at most 32 size-adjusted groups. The same identity-link noise models
are available as in `splogconNMF()`, including negative binomial and Gamma
models. The [PSF help page](../reference/estimate_psf.html) describes likelihood
fitting, noise scaling and aggregation.

`GCMSdeco()` uses the same estimator. A CDF contains the sample chromatogram;
its accompanying R calibration attribute can be supplied explicitly:

```r
calibrated <- GCMSdeco(file.path(out, "GCMS_data2.cdf"),
  file.path(out, "GCMS_data2_calibrated.msp"), nwindows = 3L, precluster = 32L,
  psf_control = list(standard = attr(GCMS_data2, "alkanes_TIC")))
```

Calibration peaks should reflect the sample's chromatographic conditions.
The bundled beer calibration has broader peaks than the PSF used in the
plotted comparison, so the table and figures below use the explicit Gaussian
PSFs in `fit1` and `fit2` above. Automatic calibration is available through
the calls in this section.

<!-- BEGIN gcms-results -->
These results were obtained with the calls above on the [benchmark workstation](performance.html#reproduce-and-extend), using eight OpenMP workers and one BLAS thread. Timings are medians of two complete runs, including CDF reading, PSF initialization, factorization and MSP export.

| Dataset | Scans | Mass channels | Compounds | Time (s) | GIC | Adjusted weighted R² |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `GCMS_data1` | 119 | 671 | 6 | 4.77 | 219,686 | 0.98980 |
| `GCMS_data2` | 1,764 | 518 | 37 | 92.21 | 1,289,044 | 0.99418 |

Weighted R² uses weights `1/pmax(fitted_mean, 0.1)` and a separate weighted mean for each ion channel. Its adjustment is conditional on the fitted profiles, using the positive spectral coefficients and background coefficients as the parameter count.

## Plot and export the results

```r
plot(fit1, type = "lines", nrows = 1L,
  minutes_per_panel = diff(range(fit1$time)) + 0.01, labels = TRUE)
plot(fit1, type = "heatmap")
plot(fit1, type = "profiles", nrows = 3L)

plot(fit2, type = "lines", file = file.path(out, "GCMS_data2_traces.pdf"),
  nrows = 1L, minutes_per_panel = diff(range(fit2$time)) + 0.01)
plot(fit2, type = "heatmap", file = file.path(out, "GCMS_data2_heatmaps.pdf"))
plot(fit2, type = "profiles", file = file.path(out, "GCMS_data2_profiles_and_spectra.pdf"),
  nrows = 3L)
```

Grey traces show individual observed ion signals after subtracting the fitted
background. Coloured curves show the fitted compounds, scaled by their
strongest ion; the square-root display makes weak peaks easier to inspect.
The four raster heatmaps show the observations, background-corrected
observations, fitted chromatogram and Pearson residuals. Red vertical lines
mark compound apices. Profile-and-spectrum panels follow increasing apex
retention time; `order="area"` displays the largest compounds first.

Supply `xlsx_file=file.path(out, "GCMS_data2.xlsx")` when fitting to also export
the compound table and integrated areas. Each spectrum occupies one unwrapped
cell, with fragments ordered by intensity. The returned object stores the
source CDF path rather than a second copy of the observed chromatogram;
plotting reloads the required scans from that file.

## Fit a supplied PSF design directly

Use `splogconNMF()` when a suitable PSF design and background basis are already
available. This also gives direct control over the background for a short
chromatographic window:

```r
Y <- GCMS_data1
X <- convmatrix(convkernel("gaussian", 65L, list(sigma = 8)), nrow(Y))
B <- matrix(1, nrow(Y), 1L)          # constant background in this short window
nmf <- splogconNMF(X, Y, background = B,
  family = quasipoisson("identity"), precluster = 16L,
  correlation = "none", ncores = 8L)
nmf$rank
nmf$H                              # unit-sum, log-concave profiles
coef(nmf)                          # full-channel integrated intensities
GIC(nmf)
```

For `GCMS_data2`, a low-dimensional nonnegative spline background can be
constructed with `splines::bs(as.numeric(rownames(Y)), df=4L, intercept=TRUE)`.
Quasipoisson is useful for instrumental intensities with extra variation;
Poisson, Gaussian, negative binomial and Gamma signal models are also
available. See [the likelihood and shape-constraint details](log-concave-nmf.html).

## Algorithm

For observed scan-by-mass matrix \(Y\), the mean is

\[
\mu=HS+BA+O,\qquad H,S,A\geq0,\qquad
\sum_iH_{ir}=1,\quad\Delta^2\log H_{\cdot r}\leq0.
\]

Each column of \(H\) is one compound's elution profile and each row of \(S\)
is its spectrum. The low-df basis \(B\) models background; \(O\) is a known
offset when supplied to `splogconNMF()`. The criterion is

\[
J=-2\sum_{ij}w_{ij}\ell(y_{ij};\mu_{ij},\nu)
   +m\kappa\lambda_{IC}K,
\]

where \(K\) is the compound count, \(m\) the **original** channel count and
\(\nu\) the shared noise parameters. Dividing this criterion by \(m\) gives
one rank penalty per compound. Background and profile complexity have no
additional penalty. For quasi families, the likelihood kernel and IC are
scaled by the common dispersion. The optional temporal working adjustment
\(\kappa=1+2\widehat\rho_1\) is held fixed during rank comparisons;
`correlation="none"` sets \(\kappa=1\).

1. Estimate a shared marginal noise scale from temporal differences, and
   calibrate the PSF from the sample or an alkane standard.
2. Cluster ion traces after adjusting for their total intensity. With
   `precluster=32L`, sum the channels into at most 32 groups.
3. Fit grouped adaptive ridge on the shifted PSF design and unpenalized
   background. Fuse spectrally compatible overlapping components when their
   combined profile is log-concave and the compound-count criterion improves.
4. Lift the spectra and background to all original channels. Refit their
   coefficients using the original observations and noise model.
5. Refine local log-concave profiles and spectra, treating all other compounds
   as offsets. Consider broad-anchor and compatible-tail fusions, restoring
   distinct components when the full criterion favours them. A narrow fragment
   contained within a spectrally matching broad profile can also receive a
   guarded whole-profile refit with a shared background update. Neighbouring
   modes remain within one quarter of their starting FWHM; the complete
   original-channel criterion must decrease for the fusion to be retained.
6. Apply the conservative broad-profile fusion pass, refine the affected
   neighbourhoods, and return profiles and spectra in temporal order.

The same original-channel compound penalty is used in the reduced-space
search. Native Rcpp/OpenMP kernels share the sparse profile design and update
only the local scan windows. Candidate clustering uses algebraic spectral
and profile calculations; likelihood refits are reserved for proposed model
changes and final refinement.

## Mathematical background and references

The model is a sparse log-concave nonnegative
[generalized matrix factorization](https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxag010),
with an identity link and a smooth background. Its loss gives the connection to
[deviance matrix factorization](https://doi.org/10.1214/23-EJS2174), with
rank selection and shape constraints. For standard fixed-parameter
exponential-family models its likelihood loss is a weighted Bregman
divergence, giving the connection to
[Bregman NMF](https://doi.org/10.3390/s23167229).
The [derivation and noise-specific divergences](log-concave-nmf.html#deviance-matrix-factorization-and-bregman-nmf)
are given in the mathematical article.

Sparse deconvolution with shifted peak shapes follows the idea of
[de Rooi & Eilers (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2011.05.030).
Adaptive ridge selection is related to
[Frommlet & Nuel (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0148620).
Size-adjusted Poisson clustering builds on
[Witten (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1214/11-AOAS493), while the Poisson likelihood
connects to KL-divergence NMF as studied by
[Lee & Seung (2000)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2000/file/f9d1152547c0bde01830b7e8bd60024c-Paper.pdf).
Log-concave profile modelling is inspired by
[Eilers (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1002/cem.935).

The combination of grouped selection, pooled noise calibration, local
original-scale likelihood updates, hard log-concavity and compound-count
fusion is developed for L0glm. The
[sparse log-concave NMF article](log-concave-nmf.html#local-quadratic-updates)
derives its score, working information, constrained profile updates and
likelihood acceptance rules.

The experimental data are described in [Van Oystaeyen et al. (2014)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1244899)
and [Schreurs et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-46346-0).
